To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Commonwealth government has been able to have extensive intrusions into the independence of the auditor-general accepted largely as benign or untainted by political interest.
the executive encroachment on the independence of the auditor-general is pervasive and that the independence of the Commonwealth auditor-general is not substantive.
there is a need for an audit office that is independent of political and administrative influences and that the independence of the auditor-general is the key to achieving such an office.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the extent to which the Commonwealth Auditor-General's Office (the Office) can be considered as independent.

the extent of executive encroachment on the independence of the Commonwealth Auditor- General, with particular reference to the role of the Auditor-General in the Commonwealth's accountability arrangements, the extent of executive influence over the appointment and removal of the Auditor-General, the extent of the influence of the executive over the audit program and the extent to which the Auditor-General's reports and other public communications are subject to executive influence.
the extent and nature of executive encroachments on the independence of the Commonwealth Auditor- General.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the executive has been able to have a very extensive executive intrusiveness in the public sector audit function accepted largely as benign, untainted by political considerations and maintaining an illusion of unfettered, autonomy in public sector audit.

the Commonwealth government has been able to have extensive executive intrusions into public sector audit accepted as benign and untarnished by political interests, and has thereby maintained an illusion of an unencumbered and autonomous public sector audit.

the Commonwealth Auditor-General's Office has never been independent in the sense that the office is free of political influence, and that it is not independent in the sense of being free of executive interference.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there has been a failure of imagination, a failure of vision and a failure of leadership.

the executive has been able to encroach upon the auditor-general’s independence in a variety of ways, and that these encroachments have been largely tolerated by the public, by the profession and by the legislature.

the Commonwealth government has been able to maintain the illusion of an independent public sector audit function through the creation of a series of conditions and constraints on the auditor-general's office which, in the main, are not apparent to the public or to the parliament.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the independence of the public sector auditor-general is not a simple concept and is not easily achieved in practice.
the independence of the Commonwealth Auditor- General is not what we thought it to be, but what we thought it was is not what we ought to have thought it was.
the independence of the public sector auditor-general is not an absolute concept but is a relative concept that is contingent on the circumstances and context in which the auditor-general operates.
